title: Kabandha's curse
hookLine: the monster's shape was a prank that became a curse
carry: as you act, so you become
last: THE SELF IS NOT THE BODY.

cards: Lying armless on the forest floor, the creature that tried to eat them sounds almost grateful. Kabandha tells the brothers his story, and it isn't a monster's story at all.
Once, he says, he was radiant and beautiful, as bright as the moon. And he had a habit: he liked to put on a terrifying shape and jump out at the sages in the forest, to frighten them.
One day he frightened the wrong sage.

teach.h: A SAGE'S CURSE: KEEP THAT SHAPE.
teach.b: The sage was Sthulashira, and he was not amused. Since you love that shape so much, he said, keep it.
Kabandha begged, and the sage softened the curse: it would end the day Rama cut off his arms and burned his body in the forest. More trouble followed.

Proud of his strength, Kabandha attacked Indra, king of the gods, and Indra's thunderbolt drove his head and thighs into his body. That's why he has no head. The shape he wore as a joke became the shape he was stuck in.
This is karma, and it isn't what most people think. Karma isn't cosmic revenge.

The word simply means action. Hindus teach that every action bears fruit, and the first place it ripens is in the one who does it. An old Upanishad, the Brihadaranyaka, says it plainly: as a person acts, so he becomes.

teach.h: AS YOU ACT, SO YOU BECOME.
teach.b: Doing good, one becomes good; doing bad, one becomes bad. Kabandha didn't get a random punishment. He got more of what he kept choosing.
But the curse had a second half: an end, and the end was Rama. In Hindu stories a curse often comes with its release, and many teachers read that as grace meeting karma.
So Kabandha asks: burn me, and I'll tell you how to find Sita. Once more the brothers build a pyre, for a creature who tried to eat them.
From the fire he rises bright, in shining clothes, in a chariot in the air: his old self, finally visible. And he gives them a plan. Find Sugriva, the exiled monkey on Mount Rishyamuka.
And on the way, an old woman named Shabari. She's been waiting.

how: In Hindu stories a curse (shapa) often comes with its release; Kabandha's ends through Rama's sword and a proper funeral, and teachers use him to show karma as what our own actions make of us.

o: a forest sage who curses anyone who dares to frighten him
a cursed being who keeps the scary shape he wore as a prank
a monkey king driven out by his own brother Vali

p: action, and what it makes of you
as you act, so you become
the friend he tells Rama to find

s: karma is a punishment someone hands out to you
karma means action; actions bear their own fruit, and the Upanishad says they shape who you become.
he was radiant once, and a sage's curse fixed him in the shape he used to frighten people.
Kabandha asks the brothers to burn his body
the curse ends with the fire, and he rises in a bright form.

games.q: your cousin keeps 'just pretending' to be mean so he looks tough. what would the Upanishad say?
o: it's harmless; it's only an act.
careful: as you act, so you become.
karma only counts for the big stuff, not pretending.
games.why: Kabandha's prank shape became his real shape. Karma isn't a punishment from outside; it starts with what our actions make of us.

practice: Think of one thing you've done again and again this week, kind or not. Breathe in and ask: what is this making me? Breathe out and choose one small action for tomorrow that you'd like to become.
If you pray, offer it the way Krishna asks in the Gita: whatever you do, do it as an offering. If not, just hold the choice.

wordCard.voice: Kabandha. Cursed to keep the frightening shape he wore as a prank, until Rama freed him through fire.

orig.note: Sanskrit śāpa: a curse. this one comes with a way out: Rama.

carryVoice: Your line: as you act, so you become. Someone has been waiting a long time. Until tomorrow.
